stories.head: Squamish River forecast to see its biggest flood since 2003 by Wednesday night: 1 in 10 year, and it could near 1 in 50
stories.dek: The province's river model has the Squamish River reaching a flow not seen since 2003. The middle forecast is a 1 in 10 to 1 in 20 year flood. The range runs from an ordinary yearly high to just under 1 in 50. The Upper Squamish Valley has no dikes and one road out. Most of town sits behind dikes. Six charts, every number, and what to do before Tuesday night.
stories.take: The Squamish River is forecast to rise fast early Wednesday and be near its peak from Wednesday evening through Thursday, about 2,231 cubic metres per second, with a possible range of about 1,360 to 2,784. A provincial Flood Watch is in effect, which means flooding is possible, not certain.
stories.body:
## The short version

- **Who is at risk:** the Upper Squamish Valley, the rural valley along Squamish Valley Road north of town. It has no dikes and one road in and out. Paradise Valley is also exposed.
- **Do now:** if you are on low ground in the Upper Squamish Valley or Paradise Valley, move animals, vehicles, trailers and feed in daylight on Tuesday.
- **In town:** most of town sits behind dikes, which lower the risk but do not remove it. This story is mostly about the valleys upriver. In town, expect very heavy rain, pooled water on roads and closed river trails.
- **How big:** the province's river model has the Squamish River peaking near **2,231 cubic metres per second** at the gauge near Brackendale. On the province's own scale that is between a 1 in 10 and a 1 in 20 year flood, and it would be the highest flow since the October 2003 flood.
- **A way to picture it:** the middle forecast is about 10% more water than the January 2024 high water. The top of the forecast range is closer to the 2003 flood than to 2024.
- **How bad it could get:** the top of the range is 2,784, just under a 1 in 50 year flood.
- **How mild it could be:** the bottom of the range is about 1,360, the kind of high water the river sees every second year.
- **Highway, schools, power and Remembrance Day:** as of Monday night, Highway 99 is clear and no school closures are announced. Details are under "What to do" below.

A Flood Watch is in effect. That means flooding is possible, not certain.

**The timeline.** This is the province's forecast for the Squamish River:

- **Monday night:** the river was at 237 and falling. It is calm before the rain.
- **Tuesday, November 10:** heavy rain starts, but the river stays low most of the day, around 200 to 300.
- **Overnight Tuesday into Wednesday:** the river starts climbing fast.
- **Wednesday morning, about 6 a.m.:** past 1,000 and still rising quickly. Wednesday is Remembrance Day, and the [ceremony at the cenotaph](/news/squamish-remembrance-day-ceremony-2026/) falls in the heaviest rain.
- **Wednesday afternoon, about 4 p.m.:** past 2,000.
- **Wednesday evening, about 7 p.m.:** past the 1 in 10 year mark of 2,129, and already within about 4% of the peak.
- **Thursday, November 12, morning:** the peak, near 2,231.
- **If the high end of the forecast comes true:** the river is past the 1 in 10 year mark by about 6 a.m. Wednesday, half a day sooner.
- **Thursday evening:** still around 2,000.
- **Friday morning:** back under 1,300 and falling.
- **Saturday:** a second, smaller bump near 850 from Friday's rain.

The river is forecast to stay above 2,000 for about 28 hours, from Wednesday afternoon to Thursday evening. Do not read "peak Thursday morning" as having until Thursday: the river is forecast to be almost as high by Wednesday evening.

You can see the province's own chart for the Squamish River [here](https://bcrfc.env.gov.bc.ca/freshet/clever/08GA022.PDF). It was issued at 10:11 a.m. Monday, November 9. The province reruns it at least once a day, so check the time stamp on the chart. River numbers in this story come from that forecast unless we say otherwise. Rain and freezing level numbers come from the Open-Meteo weather model.

One caution: these numbers are flow at the gauge. Flow does not say exactly which land floods. That depends on the water level at each spot, log jams and banks giving way.

## Who is most exposed

- **Upper Squamish Valley.** This is the rural valley north of Brackendale, not the town. The homes, farms and campgrounds along Squamish Valley Road have no dikes. The regional district's [2018 flood study](https://www.slrd.bc.ca/media/file/squamishfloodhazardreportfinalr4-maps-and-appendixpdf) maps large parts of the valley floor under water in a 1 in 50 year flood. Squamish Valley Road is the only road in and out.
- **Paradise Valley.** The Cheakamus River is forecast to peak near 393 on Thursday afternoon, about 1.4 times its typical yearly peak of 291 and 46% of its record of 861, set in 1963. An evacuation alert was issued for Paradise Valley during the November 2021 storm.
- **Squamish town, including Brackendale.** The gauge is named for Brackendale because it sits on the river nearby. That does not mean Brackendale is forecast to flood. Most of town sits behind dikes, which lower the risk but do not remove it. The District keeps raising them under its flood plan. We track that work on our [flood protection page](/issues/flood-protection/). High water still closes trails, floods low spots and makes riverbanks dangerous.
- **Mamquam River.** Forecast to peak near 358 late Wednesday. That is 83% of its record of 431, set in 1990, and the top of its forecast range is 433, a hair over the record.
- **Elaho River.** Forecast to peak near 1,106 Wednesday afternoon. That is 76% of its record of 1,450, set in January 2024, and the top of its forecast range is 1,477, also over the record. The Elaho is forecast lower than in January 2024 while the Squamish is forecast higher, which would mean more of the water comes from the other creeks and rivers along the valley this time.
- **Stawamus River and small creeks.** The province does not publish a forecast for these. Small, steep creeks rise and fall within hours, and the Flood Watch says they are especially sensitive.
- **Squamish Nation communities.** Several Squamish Nation reserves sit beside these rivers. The Nation runs its own alert system for members. Check the Nation's channels for its updates.

## What to do

**If you live in the Upper Squamish Valley or Paradise Valley:**

- **Move animals, trailers, vehicles, feed and equipment off low ground in daylight on Tuesday.** The river is forecast to start climbing overnight Tuesday.
- **If being cut off would put you at risk, leave in daylight on Tuesday.** That means medical needs, small children or no supplies. Squamish Valley Road is the only way out and can flood before your property does. Do not count on leaving Wednesday.
- **If an evacuation order is issued, leave at once.**
- **Otherwise, be ready to be cut off.** Have three days of food, water, medicine and fuel, and charge your phones. Power and internet often go out up the valley.
- **Sign up for alerts now.** Upper Squamish Valley and upper Paradise Valley: [SLRD Alert](https://www.slrd.bc.ca/SLRDAlert). Town and lower Paradise Valley: [Squamish Alert](https://squamish.ca/alert). If you are not sure which covers you, sign up for both.
- **Know the two evacuation words.** An evacuation alert means be ready to leave. An evacuation order means leave now.

**Phone numbers, in case the internet is down:**

- **Emergency:** 911
- **Squamish Lillooet Regional District** (handles the Upper Squamish Valley and upper Paradise Valley): 1-800-298-7753
- **District of Squamish public works, for flooding in town:** 604-815-6868, after hours 604-815-4040
- **DriveBC road reports:** 1-800-550-4997
- **BC Hydro, power out or a line down:** 1-800-224-9376

**Highway, schools, power and Remembrance Day, as of 11:15 p.m. Monday:**

- **Highway 99:** no incidents or closures between Horseshoe Bay and Whistler on [DriveBC](https://www.drivebc.ca/). Live status is on our [Today page](/today/).
- **Schools:** Wednesday is a holiday. For Thursday, the Sea to Sky School District says schools stay open unless a closure is announced, and families are told by 7 a.m. Check [sd48seatosky.org](https://www.sd48seatosky.org/).
- **Power:** heavy rain and wind bring outages. The outage map is at [bchydro.com](https://www.bchydro.com/power-outages/app/outage-map.html).
- **Remembrance Day:** the [ceremony at the cenotaph](/news/squamish-remembrance-day-ceremony-2026/) is outdoors, just before 11 a.m. Wednesday, in the heaviest rain. We have not seen any change announced. Check with the [Legion](https://www.squamishlegion.ca).

**For everyone:**

- **Never drive through water on a road.** You cannot see how deep it is or whether the road is still there.
- **Stay off riverbanks, dike edges and gravel bars** from Tuesday night to Friday. Banks can give way under fast water.
- **Clear leaves from the storm drains** near your home before the heavy rain, never in moving water.
- **Follow the official sources.** The regional district's emergency page is [slrd.bc.ca/emergency-program](https://www.slrd.bc.ca/emergency-program). The District of Squamish's is [squamish.ca](https://squamish.ca/public-safety-services/emergency-program/). Evacuation alerts and orders across BC are on [EmergencyInfoBC](https://www.emergencyinfobc.gov.bc.ca/). The province's flood guide is at [PreparedBC](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/safety/emergency-management/preparedbc/know-your-hazards/floods).

## How big is 2,231?

River flow is measured in cubic metres of water passing the gauge each second. These are the flood sizes the BC River Forecast Centre uses for the Squamish River near Brackendale:

- **Every second year:** 1,351
- **1 in 5 year flood:** 1,809
- **1 in 10 year flood:** 2,129
- **1 in 20 year flood:** 2,441
- **1 in 50 year flood:** 2,843
- **1 in 100 year flood:** 3,137
- **October 2003, the biggest on record:** 3,140

The middle forecast of 2,231 is past the 1 in 10 year mark. The top of the range, 2,784, is 59 short of the 1 in 50 year mark.

**The ten biggest floods on record.** The gauge has 61 published yearly peaks going back to 1958, from Water Survey of Canada. Seven years (1967, 1992, 1996, 2016, 2017, 2019 and 2020) have no published peak flow. For 2016, the recorded water level suggests a peak of about 2,000, which would put it on this list:

- **1. October 18, 2003:** 3,140
- **2. October 8, 1984:** 2,610
- **3. August 30, 1991:** 2,460
- **4. November 1, 1981:** 2,270
- **5. December 27, 1980:** 2,180
- **6. September 20, 2015:** 2,080
- **7. November 12, 1990:** 2,060
- **8. January 30, 2024:** 2,010
- **9. November 5, 1975:** 1,950
- **10. October 12, 1958:** 1,880

Where this storm would land on that list:

- **Middle forecast, 2,231:** fifth biggest of the 61 recorded yearly peaks, and the biggest since 2003.
- **Top of the range, 2,784:** second only to 2003.
- **Bottom of the range, about 1,360:** an ordinary year. The river peaked higher than that in 2021 (1,660) and last December (1,510).

Nine of the ten biggest floods came between late August and December. Only five years on record have passed the 1 in 10 year mark of 2,129: 1980, 1981, 1984, 1991 and 2003. None since. A "1 in 10 year flood" does not mean it comes every ten years. It means a one in ten chance in any single year.

## The rain behind it

- **Environment Canada's warning:** 120 to 160 mm in Squamish from early Tuesday to Wednesday night, possibly more, with moderate rain into Thursday morning.
- **The mountains get more.** The Open-Meteo weather model puts about 76 mm on the Elaho headwaters Tuesday, 119 mm Wednesday and 55 mm Thursday. That is about 250 mm in three days on the ground that feeds the river.
- **The valley floor:** about 68 mm Tuesday, 57 mm Wednesday and 46 mm Thursday in the same model.
- **It follows a wet week.** The same model puts about 156 mm on the headwaters in the seven days before this storm.

## It keeps raining Friday. Why does the river peak Thursday?

A river does not peak when the rain stops. It peaks after the heaviest and warmest rain.

- **Tuesday and Wednesday are the big days.** Rain on the headwaters drops by half on Thursday and to under 20 mm on Friday.
- **Those days are also warm.** The freezing level is forecast to climb to about 2,900 metres. That is above most of the peaks, so it rains on nearly the whole watershed instead of snowing on the top half. The province's Flood Watch also warns of melt from the shallow early snowpack.
- **The river lags the rain.** The Elaho is forecast to peak Wednesday afternoon. Its water reaches Brackendale within hours and drives the Wednesday evening rise. Continued rain then holds the river up into Thursday.
- **Thursday's rain is lighter.** Once the rain eases, less water is arriving than the river is carrying away, so it falls even though it is still raining. This watershed is steep and rocky and drains in about a day.
- **Friday is colder.** The freezing level falls to roughly 1,400 metres on Friday morning, so the upper half of the watershed gets snow, and snow stays on the mountain.

One thing to watch: forecasts disagree about how much rain falls Friday. If it comes in wetter and warmer, Saturday's second bump would be bigger than forecast, on ground that is already soaked.

## The ground and the water table

Until last week it had been a dry fall. A provincial groundwater monitoring well on Paradise Valley Road hit its lowest level since readings began in 2015 at the end of October: 8.67 metres below the ground.

Then the rain came. The Open-Meteo weather model puts about 156 mm on the Squamish River headwaters in the last seven days, and the Squamish River briefly reached about 800 on Sunday. The well has risen half a metre in a week and is still well below normal for November.

What that means: this one well only tells us about Paradise Valley, and it says the ground there started this storm unusually dry underneath. It cannot tell us about the Upper Squamish Valley. As a general rule, the water table in river gravels rises with the river, so low ground and old channels beside a river can get wet before any water comes over the banks.

## Where the flood call comes from

When the District of Squamish or the regional district says there might be a flood, they are passing on a notice from the BC River Forecast Centre. The province builds it in four steps:

- **Rain forecast.** Weather models say how much rain lands on the mountains, hour by hour.
- **Freezing level and snow.** Warm storms rain on the whole watershed and melt snow. Cold storms leave snow up high.
- **River model.** The rain, the melt and the current river flow go into a model that predicts flow at each gauge for ten days.
- **Compare with past floods.** The predicted peak is compared with flood sizes, and one of three notices goes out.

The three notices, from mildest to most serious:

- **High Streamflow Advisory:** rivers rising fast, no major flooding expected.
- **Flood Watch:** rivers may reach or go over the top of their banks.
- **Flood Warning:** rivers are over their banks, or will be very soon.

Squamish is under the middle one. The province upgraded the South Coast, including Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky, to a [Flood Watch](https://bcrfc.env.gov.bc.ca/warnings/advisories/FWT_2026_11_09_1236_SC-NVI-WVI-CVI-East%20Vancouver%20Island-CC%20-%20Kingcome-Fraser%20Valley-North_UPG.pdf) at 12:36 p.m. Monday.

## How this compares with the official bulletin

Here is how the river forecast sits beside what agencies and other news outlets have said so far:

- **Environment Canada** has an orange rainfall warning for Squamish to Whistler: 120 to 160 mm, possibly more, with flooding likely and some roads possibly impassable. We covered that [here](/news/rainfall-warning-160-mm-squamish-2/).
- **The province's Flood Watch** covers the whole South Coast and Vancouver Island in general words. It says modelling shows "the potential for flows in the 5-year to 10-year range, or higher, in areas".
- **The Squamish Chief and North Shore News** have reported the rainfall warning. Other outlets have reported the Flood Watch for the coast as a whole.
The bulletin covers the whole coast, so it does not name single rivers. The forecast for each river sits one layer deeper on the province's website, as a chart for each gauge. For the Squamish River, that chart falls in the "or higher" part of the bulletin's line: the middle forecast is over the 1 in 10 year mark, and the top of the range is close to 1 in 50.

## What could change

- **This is a model, not a promise.** The forecast range is very wide, from about 1,360 to 2,784. The province says the real flow can even land outside that range.
- **It will be updated.** The province reruns the forecast at least once a day. If the storm tracks north or south, or the freezing level changes, the peak moves with it.
- **A Flood Warning would be the next step.** If the province issues one for the Squamish River, flooding is expected, not just possible.

We will update this story when the province issues a new forecast.

stories.head: Up to 160 mm of rain hits Squamish Tuesday. Here's what to expect
stories.dek: Squamish could get 120 to 160 mm of rain, or more, starting early Tuesday morning. Environment Canada has issued a rainfall warning for Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky from Squamish to Whistler. Heavy rain lasts until Wednesday night, with more rain into Thursday morning.
stories.take: Expect 120 to 160 mm of rain from early Tuesday to Wednesday night, with flooding likely and some roads possibly impassable; check DriveBC before you travel.
stories.body:
## What to expect

Environment Canada has issued a rainfall warning for Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky from Squamish to Whistler. Very heavy rain is expected.

- **How much:** 120 to 160 mm, possibly more
- **Starts:** early Tuesday morning
- **Heaviest rain:** Tuesday until overnight Wednesday
- **Ends:** moderate rain continues until Thursday morning

Environment Canada says a very strong weather front is set to reach Vancouver Island overnight Monday. Rain, at times heavy, will last until overnight Wednesday. Even after the heaviest rain eases, moderate rain will continue into Thursday morning. That could push the total to 150 mm or higher.

## The risks

The warning lists several possible effects:

- Local flooding is likely
- Some roads may become impassable
- Visibility may suddenly drop at times
- Landslides may happen in vulnerable areas, such as steep slopes, areas where trees have been cut, or recent burn scars

Weather in the mountains can change suddenly, which can make driving hazardous.

## Before you travel

- Check road conditions at [DriveBC](https://www.drivebc.ca/)
- See current weather, Highway 99, river and air conditions on our [Today page](/today/)
- Read more about local flood risk on our [flood protection issue page](/issues/flood-protection/)

## Stay updated

Environment Canada asks people to keep watching its alerts and forecasts. You can report severe weather by emailing BCstorm@ec.gc.ca or posting on social media with #BCStorm.

Read the full warning on the [Environment Canada website](https://weather.gc.ca/warnings/index_e.html?prov=bc).

stories.head: Council drops closed Nov 10 meeting so its next business meeting is public
stories.dek: The new council's second business meeting was going to be a closed session for legal advice on November 10. Councillors asked to change the schedule, so their next business meeting is now the public one on Tuesday, November 17 at 6 p.m.
stories.take: The November 10 closed meeting is cancelled. The new council's next business meeting is the public one on Tuesday, November 17 at 6 p.m. in Council Chambers, and you can attend or watch live.
stories.body:
## What changed

The District of Squamish has cancelled the [special business meeting](/meetings/2026-11-10-special/) that was set for Tuesday, November 10 at 9 a.m. The District's meeting listing now reads "MEETING CANCELLED" and gives no reason.

That meeting would have been almost entirely private. Its only item was a vote to close the doors so council could get legal advice from its lawyers, which is protected by solicitor and client privilege. Residents could have watched the opening minutes and nothing more.

## Why council asked for the change

Councillor [Laura Prosko](/council/laura-prosko/) explained the change in a statement that former council candidate Anders Ourom shared in a local Facebook group:

"We didn't want our first meeting as a new Council to be a closed meeting, so we requested a change to the schedule with the CAO. We now have an orientation and meeting scheduled for Tuesday, November 10, at 9 am. We felt it was important to ensure our first meeting aligned with our commitment to transparency, and that's why we made the change."

The CAO is the chief administrative officer, the District's top staff member, who sets up council's meeting schedule.

What this means:

- The new council still meets staff on November 10, but for an orientation. It is not listed as a public meeting.
- The council's next business meeting is now **Tuesday, November 17**, and it is open to the public.
- The council was sworn in on November 3. That [inaugural meeting](/meetings/2026-11-03-inaugural/) was a ceremony and also a business meeting: it had an agenda, and council voted on its regional district board members, the acting mayor rotation, appointments to other boards and its 2027 meeting schedule. Those votes are on the public record.

## Where and when: November 17

- **What:** [Regular council meeting](/meetings/2026-11-17-regular/), the new council's first regular business meeting
- **When:** Tuesday, November 17, starting at 6 p.m.
- **Where:** Council Chambers, Municipal Hall, 37955 Second Avenue
- **Open to the public:** yes, anyone can attend in person
- **Watch live:** [District of Squamish YouTube streams](https://www.youtube.com/@DistrictofSquamish/streams)
- **Agenda:** usually posted the Thursday before on the [District's meeting portal](https://squamish.civicweb.net/Portal/MeetingInformation.aspx?Id=2119). We will explain every item in plain language on our [meeting page](/meetings/2026-11-17-regular/) once it posts.

## Who is on the new council

- [Mayor Sean Easton](/council/sean-easton/)
- [Councillor Eric Andersen](/council/eric-andersen/)
- [Councillor Janice DesJardins](/council/janice-desjardins/)
- [Councillor Sarah Ellis](/council/sarah-ellis/)
- [Councillor Luc Perreault](/council/luc-perreault/)
- [Councillor Laura Prosko](/council/laura-prosko/)
- [Councillor Shaun Veltkamp](/council/shaun-veltkamp/)

You can follow how their votes line up with their campaign promises on our [scorecard](/scorecard/). New to local government? Read our [plain guide to how council works](/how-council-works/).

stories.head: Power out for 2,152 Squamish customers since 2:38 a.m. Sunday
stories.dek: More than 2,000 BC Hydro customers in Squamish lost power early Sunday morning. The outage began at 2:38 a.m. on November 8 in the area south of Transit Place. The cause is under investigation, a crew is assigned, and there is no restoration estimate yet.
stories.take: Check BC Hydro's live outage map for updates, since there is no restoration estimate yet.
stories.body:
## What happened

BC Hydro reports a power outage in Squamish affecting 2,152 customers. The power went off on Sunday, November 8 at 2:38 a.m.

- Customers affected: 2,152
- Area: south of Transit Place
- Power went off: Sunday, November 8 at 2:38 a.m.
- Cause: under investigation
- Crew status: crew assigned
- Restoration estimate: none yet

## The details

BC Hydro has not said what caused the outage. It lists the cause as under investigation. A crew has been assigned to the outage, but BC Hydro has not yet given a time for when power should be back on.

This information was last updated by BC Hydro on Sunday, November 8 at 2:55 a.m. Outage numbers like these can change quickly as crews work and as power comes back to some areas before others.

## Where to check for updates

BC Hydro posts the latest details, including any restoration estimate, on its live outage map:

- [BC Hydro live outage map](https://www.bchydro.com/power-outages/app/outage-map.html)

stories.head: 50 mm of rain heads for Squamish tonight. Here's where to watch out
stories.dek: Squamish could see about 50 mm of rain from tonight through Sunday. Environment Canada has issued a rainfall warning for Howe Sound and Metro Vancouver as another strong low pressure system reaches the South Coast. Water may pool on roads, and washouts and landslides are possible in some areas.
stories.take: Expect water pooling on roads from tonight through Sunday, and take care near rivers, creeks, culverts and steep slopes.
stories.body:
## What is coming

Environment Canada issued a rainfall warning on November 7, 2026 for Howe Sound, which includes Squamish. The same warning covers Metro Vancouver, including the North Shore, West Vancouver and North Vancouver.

- **When:** tonight through Sunday
- **How much:** about 50 mm of rain
- **Why:** another strong low pressure system is heading toward the South Coast. The rain will continue until the system moves farther east.

## Where to watch out

Environment Canada says heavy rain like this can cause problems in a few kinds of places:

- **Roads and low spots:** water will likely pool on roads and in low areas.
- **Steep ground:** landslides may happen on steep slopes, in areas where trees have been cleared, and on land burned by recent fires.
- **Near water:** watch for washouts near rivers, creeks and culverts.

## Stay up to date

Environment Canada asks people to keep checking its alerts and forecasts. You can see the current warning on the [Environment Canada warnings page](https://weather.gc.ca/warnings/index_e.html?prov=bc).

For local conditions in one place, including weather, Highway 99 and the rivers, see our [Today page](/today/). For background on how Squamish manages high water, see our [flood protection issue page](/issues/flood-protection/).

stories.head: Got old Pokémon cards? Squamish's first card show is today, and it's free
stories.dek: If you have a shoebox of Pokémon cards at home, there is a place to trade them today. Roundhouse Martial Arts & Fitness hosts what its owners call Squamish's first Pokémon Card Show on Saturday, November 7, from noon to 3 p.m. It is free for visitors and vendors, at 38147 Cleveland Avenue.
stories.take: The free show runs today, November 7, from noon to 3 p.m. on the second floor at 38147 Cleveland Avenue.
stories.body:
## What's happening

Cole Smith and Candace Fan, who own Roundhouse Martial Arts & Fitness, are hosting a Pokémon Card Show at their gym today. They say it is the first of its kind in Squamish. Fans can buy, trade or just look at cards. Entry is free, and vendors do not pay to take part either.

The show is meant to be small. Half the space is set aside for vendors. The other half is for kids of all ages to trade cards and meet each other.

## Cards locals can afford

Some Pokémon cards sell for thousands of dollars, or even millions. Smith says he does not want cards like that at this show. He wants prices that make sense for local buyers, with cards at about:

- $5 to $20 for most cards
- maybe $50 for a few

"I don't want vendors with their $3,000 card," he said.

## Why he's doing it

Smith grew up with the cards. He was in Grade 4 when Pokémon came out. Like many kids, he stopped collecting, but his mom had kept his old cards in a bin. He got back into the hobby as an adult. The couple also collect Pokémon stuffed animals when they travel, and they now have a two month old daughter.

## What could come next

Smith says a few vendors from the city have already shown interest. If one or two small shows prove there is demand, he hopes to move to Totem Hall. He would like to hold a bigger convention there that also covers sports collections and other anime collectibles.

The Squamish Chief [reported on the show](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/on-today-squamish-pokemon-collectible-card-show-on-nov-7-12941202).

## Where and when

- Saturday, November 7, 2026
- Noon to 3 p.m.
- Second floor, 38147 Cleveland Avenue, Squamish (Roundhouse Martial Arts & Fitness)
- Free for visitors and vendors
- Open to collectors, new fans and kids of all ages

stories.head: Scientists want to watch Mount Garibaldi closely. No, it isn't erupting
stories.dek: Federal scientists want to start Canada's first dedicated volcano watch on the peaks around Squamish, and the regional district has backed the idea. The Squamish-Lillooet Regional District board endorsed the proposal on October 30. The five-year project would cover Mount Garibaldi, Mount Cayley and Mount Meager from April 2027, if federal funding comes through.
stories.take: Nothing changes for residents now; the regional district endorsed a federal monitoring proposal that still needs funding approval.
stories.body:
## What the project would do

The Geological Survey of Canada, part of Natural Resources Canada, wants to run a five-year project called VolCan: Towards a Canadian Volcano Observatory. It would focus on three volcanoes in the Sea to Sky: Mount Garibaldi, Mount Cayley and Mount Meager.

Under the plan, scientists would:

- Set up baseline monitoring at priority volcanoes, so they know what normal looks like
- Create notification steps and regular updates for emergency managers
- Hold workshops and emergency exercises with regional, municipal and Indigenous governments

The work would also help the federal government decide whether to create a permanent national observatory. Canada does not have one today.

## Why Squamish is in the picture

In an October 9 letter, the survey called the three peaks the most threatening volcanoes in Canada. It said debris flows and ash could reach Squamish, Whistler and Pemberton, along with Highway 99, the CN rail line, and power and communication lines.

The ratings are about possible impacts as well as activity. They do not mean an eruption is likely soon. Garibaldi and Meager are rated very high threat, and Cayley high threat.

## No sign of an eruption

Eruptions in Canada are rare. Natural Resources Canada has reported no satellite evidence of magma moving the ground at the country's volcanoes. Scientists say eruptions usually give warning signs, sometimes months or years ahead. Mount Meager had Canada's last major explosive eruption about 2,350 years ago, with ash reaching Alberta.

## What comes next

- The Squamish-Lillooet Regional District board endorsed the plan on October 30 with no one opposed. Area A director Vivian Birch-Jones moved the motion.
- The survey is applying to the Canadian Safety and Security Program for money. Funding is not confirmed.
- If approved, the project would run from April 2027 to March 2032.

The plan builds on Canada's first volcanic hazard map workshop, held in Squamish on September 15 by the survey and Simon Fraser University's Centre for Natural Hazards Research.

The Squamish Chief [reported the endorsement](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/slrd-backs-proposal-for-canadas-first-volcano-observatory-12961715). For more on local hazards, see our [flood protection](/issues/flood-protection/) page.

stories.head: Why bears near Squamish rivers are easier to surprise right now
stories.dek: Bears getting ready to hibernate are busy eating and pay less attention to what is around them. The District of Squamish says they are often near berry bushes and along waterways feeding on spawning salmon. Trail users can easily spook them in a surprise encounter.
stories.take: Bears are feeding near berry bushes and salmon streams before hibernation, so trail users should expect them there and can find the District's tips on avoiding conflicts.
stories.body:
## What is happening

Bears in the Squamish area are getting ready for winter hibernation. The District of Squamish shared this in its Wildlife Wednesday post on November 6, 2026.

At this time of year, bears spend much of their time eating. The District says they are often found:

- Near berry bushes
- Along waterways, feeding on spawning salmon

## Why it matters on the trails

When bears are focused on eating, they are less aware of what is going on around them. That means they may not notice a person coming until the last moment.

The District says bears in this state can be easily spooked by trail users in surprise encounters. A surprise meeting is what can lead to a conflict between people and wildlife.

## Who it affects

This matters most for anyone using trails near berry patches, creeks and rivers where salmon are spawning. That includes people walking, running, biking or walking dogs.

## Where to find the tips

The District has tips available on preventing conflicts between people and wildlife along trails. You can find them through the District's E-News at [squamish.ca](https://squamish.ca/government-and-administration/district-information/enews-archives/).

For current conditions around town, see our [today page](/today/). For more local safety news, see our [policing and safety](/issues/policing-and-safety/) page.

stories.head: After 120 years, Brackendale's post office is gone. Where mail goes now
stories.dek: Brackendale's post office closed for good on October 31, 2026, 120 years after it opened. Canada Post could not fill the job or find a local business to host an outlet, so the service moves to Garibaldi Highlands. The neighbourhood itself is named after its first postmaster.
stories.take: Brackendale postal service has moved to Garibaldi Highlands after the Brackendale post office closed October 31, 2026.
stories.body:
## What happened

The Brackendale post office opened on August 1, 1906, and closed on October 31, 2026. [The Squamish Chief reported](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/the-history-of-the-brackendale-post-office-12991206) on the closure and the history of the office.

Postal service for Brackendale has now moved to Garibaldi Highlands.

## Why it closed

This summer, Brackendale residents wrote to the District of Squamish and spoke to the newspaper about staff shortages at the office.

- Canada Post could not fill the open job.
- The job paid $45,000 a year for six days of work each week.
- The person in the job also had to cover the lease payments.

Before the closure, Canada Post wrote to the District saying it would keep service in Brackendale if a local business agreed to host a postal outlet. Mike Lee, who handles government and community affairs for Canada Post, said keeping a presence in the neighbourhood was the preferred outcome, but it depended on finding a willing retail partner. No partner was found.

## How Brackendale got its name

According to BC Geographical Names, the provincial database of place names, Brackendale is named after its first postmaster, Thomas Hirst Bracken. The database describes him as an elderly Englishman who also ran a general store and the Bracken Arms Hotel. He went back to England after the hotel burned down. The database lists the post office as closing July 18, 1912.

Squamish Library archives say Hughie Mills rebuilt the post office building in 1916 after a fire. The lot was first bought from the Judd family when they divided up their land.

## A century of mail

- 2002: the office began using a special ink stamp reading "winter home of the bald eagle."
- 2004: longtime employee Joyce Berg retired after almost 27 years. She and her husband owned the building, then seen as Brackendale's commercial centre.
- 2006: the office marked 100 years, noted by a postal history newsletter for stamp collectors.

The building once kept horse feed outside for farmers, and Government Road, where it sits, was once part of the Sea to Sky Highway.

The office faced closure before. Berg said residents started many petitions back then. "I almost got fired, but we kept our post office," she told the paper in 2004.

More local news: [Brackendale and other neighbourhoods](/neighbourhoods/).

stories.head: Woodfibre now plans months of flaring, not weeks. How to comment by Nov 29
stories.dek: When Woodfibre LNG was approved in 2015, start up flaring was expected to last three to four weeks. The company now says commissioning will take six to eight months, with flaring several days a week. Comments on its air emissions permit are open until November 29.
stories.take: Email comments on the air emissions permit to info@wlng.ca, copying waste.management@bc-er.ca, by November 29, or ask questions at one of four open houses.
stories.body:
## Weeks then, months now

When Woodfibre LNG was approved, its [2015 flaring report](https://projects.eao.gov.bc.ca/api/public/document/588691c3e036fb010576901c/download/Planned%20and%20Emergency%20Flaring%20Supplemental%20Report,%20June%202015..pdf) said start up and commissioning would take about three to four weeks, with flaring bursts of up to three or four days at a time. It said flaring would happen less than 3% of the time overall, never during normal operation apart from small pilot lights, and about once a year for planned maintenance.

The company's plan today, as presented at its October open house and in its new air emissions permit application, is different:

- Commissioning now runs about **six to eight months**, with flaring several days a week.
- After the first LNG cargo, about **two years** of stabilizing operations follow, with flaring decreasing.
- About **three years** after commissioning, flaring drops to less than once a month.

Woodfibre's communications director, Sean Beardow, told The Squamish Chief the company is being "very forthright" that commissioning flaring will last longer and happen more often. Tracey Saxby of My Sea to Sky said the project was approved on what she called a false premise.

## What you would see and hear

These are the company's own modelled numbers:

- **Flame:** up to 60 metres above a 134 metre flare stack, or up to 90 metres in a rare emergency.
- **Light:** 5.4 lux at Britannia Beach, 3.4 lux in Squamish and 1.3 lux at Furry Creek during flaring. A typical street light is 10 to 15 lux.
- **Noise:** up to 6 decibels louder at Britannia Beach and 2.5 decibels in Squamish and Stá7mes.
- **Smoke:** during unplanned flaring, black smoke is allowed for up to 15 minutes in any two hour window. Longer counts as non compliance.
- **Air:** Woodfibre says its modelling keeps pollution in nearby communities below B.C.'s Air Quality Objectives, and that communities will be told before flaring happens.

A University of Victoria study published in September 2025 found LNG plants worldwide flare about three times more gas during start up than in normal running, and that start up lasted about two years on average. It named Woodfibre among Canadian projects whose assessments did not model start up flaring ([summary](https://cape.ca/press_release/first-peer-reviewed-global-study-finds-three-times-more-gas-is-flared-during-lng-facilities-start-up-phase-with-proponents-in-b-c-and-canada-not-modelling-these-in-environmental-assessment/)).

In October 2025, after that study came out, Jeremy Valeriote, then the BC Green MLA for West Vancouver Sea to Sky, called on the province to stop LNG expansion, including Woodfibre, and to count flaring in emissions reporting and environmental assessments ([Squamish Chief](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/sea-to-sky-mla-calls-for-halt-to-lng-expansion-over-flaring-health-concerns-11307853)). My Sea to Sky asked the province to require full modelling of start up flaring, including for projects already approved.

## How to comment by November 29

Woodfibre filed the air emissions permit application with the BC Energy Regulator on October 28 ([announcement](https://woodfibrelng.ca/news/2026/10/29/woodfibre-lng-submits-air-emissions-permit-application-to-bc-energy-regulator/)). It covers the flares, a furnace, a thermal oxidizer, backup diesel generators and fire pumps, and plant vents.

- **Who:** anyone who thinks they may be affected by the plant's air emissions.
- **Deadline:** Sunday, November 29.
- **Email:** info@wlng.ca, with a copy to the BC Energy Regulator at waste.management@bc-er.ca. Woodfibre collects the comments and passes them to the regulator.
- **Ideas for what to ask:** a side by side of the 2015 and current flaring plans, full emissions totals for commissioning, independent checks of noise and light, and whether the provincial Environmental Assessment Office has looked at the change.

## Open houses

Woodfibre is holding four drop in open houses on this permit and a second one for stormwater ([details](https://woodfibrelng.ca/news/2026/10/29/youre-invited-upcoming-open-houses-on-waste-discharge-authorization-wda-permit-applications/)):

- **Britannia Beach Community Hall,** 101 Church Street: Tuesday, November 17 and Wednesday, December 2, 4:30 to 7:30 p.m.
- **Executive Suites,** 40900 Tantalus Road, Squamish: Thursday, November 19 and Thursday, December 3, 4:30 to 7:30 p.m.

The Squamish Chief [reported the open house details and flaring figures](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/udpate-public-comment-period-open-for-woodfibre-lng-air-emissions-application-12855424). More background is on our [Woodfibre LNG page](/issues/woodfibre-lng/).

stories.head: Squamish's Jenna Stoner led B.C.'s towns and cities. Why she's been replaced
stories.dek: Jenna Stoner, elected president of the Union of BC Municipalities in September, has been replaced because she no longer sits on Squamish council. Fraser Lake Mayor Sarrah Storey takes over for 2026 to 2027. Stoner's loss to Mayor Sean Easton also ends her roles on the regional district and hospital district boards.
stories.take: Mayor Sean Easton and Councillors Sarah Ellis and Eric Andersen will represent Squamish on the Squamish-Lillooet Regional District board, which first meets November 26.
stories.body:
## Why Stoner was replaced

Jenna Stoner was elected president of the Union of BC Municipalities at its yearly convention in September. The group's bylaws say its leaders must hold a seat on a local council. Stoner ran for mayor of Squamish in the October 17 local elections and lost to [Mayor Sean Easton](/council/sean-easton/). Since she no longer sits on council, the union had to replace her.

In a news release, the union thanked Stoner for her years on its board and her commitment to her community. It also thanked all board members who were not re-elected this fall.

The Squamish Chief [reported the change](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/fraser-lake-mayor-succeeds-squamishs-jenna-stoner-as-head-of-ubcm-12986175).

## Who leads the union now

- **Sarrah Storey**, who had been first vice president, is now president for the 2026 to 2027 term. She was re-elected Mayor of Fraser Lake on October 17.
- **Keith Pagel**, a Nelson councillor, moves up to first vice president.

The union is more than 100 years old. It speaks for local governments across B.C. and brings their concerns to the provincial and federal governments as one voice.

## Stoner's time in office

- Eight years as a Squamish councillor
- Four years on the union's executive before becoming president, moving from director at large to third, second and then first vice president

Losing her council seat also means Stoner no longer serves as a Squamish director on the Squamish-Lillooet Regional District board, or as chair of the Sea to Sky Hospital District board.

## Who represents Squamish on the regional board

At the new council's [inaugural meeting](/meetings/2026-11-03-inaugural/), members voted on who will sit on the regional district board for this term:

- [Mayor Sean Easton](/council/sean-easton/)
- [Councillor Sarah Ellis](/council/sarah-ellis/)
- [Councillor Eric Andersen](/council/eric-andersen/)

The regional district board holds its own inaugural meeting on November 26. For more on how local government works, see our [plain guide to council](/how-council-works/).

stories.head: Woodfibre LNG wants to release treated stormwater into Howe Sound. How to comment
stories.dek: Woodfibre LNG says it has applied for a permit to send treated stormwater and drainage water from its plant into Howe Sound. People who may be affected can send written comments within 30 days of the last date the notice is posted. The application went to the BC Energy Regulator.
stories.take: People who may be adversely affected can send written comments to info@wlng.ca, with a copy to waste.management@bc-er.ca, within 30 days of the last date the notice is posted.
stories.body:
## What Woodfibre is asking for

Woodfibre LNG says it has applied to the BC Energy Regulator for an effluent discharge permit under British Columbia's Environmental Management Act. The company says the permit is part of getting the plant ready for commissioning, startup and future operations.

The plant is about seven kilometres southwest of Squamish. It is in the traditional territory of the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw (Squamish Nation) and the səlilwətaɬ (Tsleil-Waututh Nation).

## How the water would be handled

Woodfibre says rain and drainage water may touch equipment and work areas once the plant is running. It says the plant has separate drainage systems that sort water by how likely it is to be contaminated.

- Water from equipment areas that may hold contaminants goes to an oily water treatment system, or is trucked off site for disposal.
- The treatment system is designed to remove petroleum hydrocarbons and suspended solids.
- Treated water would flow into Howe Sound at an existing discharge point called Outfall 10.
- Woodfibre expects discharges mostly when it rains, with some during dry weather.
- The application proposes limits for petroleum hydrocarbons and suspended solids in the water released.

## How to comment

The BC Energy Regulator will review the application. A public notice, called an Environmental Protection Notice, sums up the proposed discharge, the treatment and the limits.

- Who can comment: members of the public who may be adversely affected by the discharge.
- Deadline: within 30 days of the last date the notice is posted, published, served or displayed.
- Send comments to Woodfibre LNG at info@wlng.ca, with a copy to the BC Energy Regulator at waste.management@bc-er.ca.
- A printed copy of the application will be at the Squamish Public Library.
- The full application and notice are linked from [Woodfibre's announcement](https://woodfibrelng.ca/news/2026/11/05/woodfibre-lng-submits-stormwater-and-drainage-permit-application-to-bc-energy-regulator/).

## Open houses

Woodfibre says it will hold open houses in Squamish and Britannia Beach in November and December. They will cover this application and a second permit application about air emissions. Dates and places are listed on Woodfibre's website.

This story reports Woodfibre LNG's own statement. More background is on our [Woodfibre LNG issue page](/issues/woodfibre-lng/).

stories.head: No political speeches at Squamish's Remembrance ceremony. Here's why
stories.dek: The Legion president wants November 11 to be only about thanking veterans, not about politics. The downtown ceremony at the cenotaph in Stan Clarke Park starts just before 11 a.m. and lasts about 15 to 20 minutes. Cleveland Avenue between Victoria and Main Streets closes for a few hours.
stories.take: Arrive about 15 minutes before 11 a.m. on November 11, expect Cleveland Avenue between Victoria and Main Streets to be closed for a few hours, and leave dogs at home unless they are authorized service dogs.
stories.body:
## Why no political speeches

Russ Robertson, president of the Diamond Head Branch 277 Squamish Legion, says the ceremony should not be political. He sees it as a simple way to honour people who served, including those who died and those who came home still living with what they went through. "We get one day," he said.

As a veteran, he said he is not encouraging speeches, because hearing a politician say something inaccurate is hard to sit through. Politicians are still welcome to attend, shake hands and lay a wreath. Robertson has also worked to keep the ceremony short, at about 15 to 20 minutes.

The Squamish Chief [reported the details](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/heres-what-you-might-not-know-about-the-squamish-remembrance-ceremony-12958862). Robertson said many people will likely be thinking of the soldiers killed and injured in a fire during training at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, Alberta, on October 17.

## Where and when

- Date: Wednesday, November 11
- Start: just before 11 a.m.; arrive about 15 minutes early
- Place: Squamish Cenotaph, Stan Clarke Park, 1361 Main Street, downtown
- Road closure: Cleveland Avenue between Victoria and Main Streets, for a few hours
- Dogs: please do not bring them, unless they are authorized service dogs
- Wreaths: for sale through the Legion website, [squamishlegion.ca](https://www.squamishlegion.ca)
- After the ceremony: everyone is invited to the Legion at 40194 Glenalder Place. Robertson says you do not need to be a veteran to visit.

## Poppies

- Poppies are available around town, including at Walmart, Save On Foods and Sunflower Bakery and Cafe.
- The Legion asks that they be worn on the left side, over the heart, without a pin that covers the poppy.
- Right after the ceremony, you can take off your poppy and place it on the cenotaph.
- Ed Robertson runs the poppy campaign, and treasurer Kella Tourand handles payments.

## Who makes it happen

- Jeremy Purdy plays the bugle.
- Rick Smith is the emcee.
- Angus Hilsley is parade sergeant at arms, now for three years.
- A colour party of seniors carries the Legion's flags.
- The 835 Griffin Royal Canadian Air Cadet Squadron takes part.
- Erik Yaremkewich organizes the flyover.
- Angela Woods volunteers on food service at the Legion.

## Facts of note

- The cenotaph honours those who died in 1914 to 1918 and 1939 to 1945. A second plaque for the Korean War was added later.
- Veteran banners are up downtown again, installed by Alta Lake Electric Ltd.
- The District of Squamish will fly the Lest We Forget poppy flag on Municipal Hall during Remembrance week.
- Legion membership grew from about 190 to 500 over the last year.

stories.head: Garibaldi's glaciers are vanishing fast. What it means for local salmon
stories.dek: The glaciers above Garibaldi Lake and Panorama Ridge are shrinking at an astonishing rate, a new film shows. Geologist and filmmaker Bob Turner, a former Bowen Island mayor, released "Vanishing Glaciers" on YouTube. He says the loss will affect the rivers and salmon around Squamish.
stories.take: Turner's 12 minute film "Vanishing Glaciers" is free to watch on YouTube, and he encourages people to visit the park's glaciers while they last.
stories.body:
## What it means for Squamish rivers

Turner describes glaciers as water towers. Through mid summer and into early fall, after the snowpack is mostly gone, melting glaciers keep streams running high. That matters most during the salmon spawning season.

As the glaciers shrink, that late season water goes too. Turner says salmon will be affected "in some way, shape, or form."

## The film

"Vanishing Glaciers" runs about 12 minutes. Turner walks the popular trail to Garibaldi Lake and Panorama Ridge in Garibaldi Provincial Park and looks at the glaciers along the way. He shot the footage in August 2025.

His main point is that the park's glaciers are disappearing very quickly. He calls glaciers "very sensitive sentinels to temperature rise." He notes that forecasts suggest very few glaciers, if any, will remain in the Coast Mountains of southern B.C. by 2100.

## Why the tone changed

While Turner was editing, a glacier collapse struck Nepal. According to the United Nations, more than 1,500 people died and 5,600 remain missing. About 2.2 million tonnes of debris destroyed more than 100 bridges, 13 hydropower dams and 23 schools.

Turner said the disaster made his film more sombre. He said it showed him the consequences of glacier loss can be catastrophic.

## A local focus

Turner said the federal and provincial governments are largely setting the environment aside to focus on the economy. He believes people at the local level, who value local salmon and wildlife, need to step up as protectors. The environment did not feature strongly in recent local or provincial elections. See our [climate and environment](/issues/climate-and-environment/) page for more.

## Go see them

The film ends on a hopeful note. "The goose isn't cooked. There are things we can do," Turner said. He also urges people to visit the glaciers and appreciate them while they are still there.

The film is on YouTube. [The Squamish Chief reported the story](https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/new-film-highlights-rapid-disappearance-of-garibaldi-provincial-park-glaciers-12983837).

stories.body:
## What the name means

Háhalhi7iwan means "becoming well in mind, body and spirit." The Squamish Nation says the name reflects the new department's focus on whole person wellness rooted in Sḵwx̱wú7mesh culture. It supports Members of all ages and walks alongside them through times of crisis and healing. Staff aim to centre each person and be guided by Sḵwx̱wú7mesh values and teachings.

The department has three main teams, plus workshops and programs.

## Therapy and healing

This team offers culturally safe therapy that takes trauma into account, for children, youth, adults, Elders and families. Services include:

- Mental health and substance use counselling
- Addictions support
- Family and individual therapy
- Crisis intervention and case management
- Coordinated care planning
- Therapy groups

Staff include community wellness and addictions therapists, addiction counsellors and family therapists.

## Family, culture and the land

Guided by Sḵwx̱wú7mesh teachings and traditional ways of knowing, this team supports people and families on their healing journeys.

- Land based healing practitioners offer traditional teachings, healing sessions, medicine gathering, outreach, workshops and programs that reconnect people to the land and traditional practices.
- Family wellness support workers help children, youth, adults and families.
- Support groups let children, youth, parents and caregivers connect with other Community Members.

## Outreach and crisis response

This team offers flexible support that is easy to access, through mobile outreach, crisis response, harm reduction and peer support. Its work includes overdose prevention, outreach and assessment, advocacy, referrals, drug checking and education. The Nation says the team works to support both immediate and long term action on the toxic drug crisis and its impacts on the Community.

Háhalhi7iwan also runs workshops and repeating programs for people of all ages.

## How to reach Háhalhi7iwan

- Phone: 604-982-7816
- Email: wellness@squamish.net
- More information, including how to pronounce the name: [Squamish Nation website](https://www.squamish.net/what-is-hahalhi7iwan-wellness/)

Related: [homelessness](/issues/homelessness/) and [policing and safety](/issues/policing-and-safety/).

stories.dek: Families can get photos with Santa, watch a Christmas tree lighting and join storytime at the top of the Sea to Sky Gondola this holiday season. The Spirit of the Season runs from late November into early January at the summit. Most events are free with a lift ticket or membership.

stories.body:
## What's happening

The Sea to Sky Gondola is holding its Spirit of the Season at the summit. Visitors can take an afternoon walk on the decorated Spirit Trail, join a storytelling session, sit by the fire and have hot chocolate and local food in the festive lodge.

The event page lists the season as November 29 to December 31 in one place and November 27, 2026 to January 3, 2027 in another. Activities run during operating hours.

## The schedule

- **Photos with Santa:** November 27 to 30 and December 4 to 7, 9:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m., Summit Lodge. You must book ahead. It costs $30 for one photo or $40 for two. The lift ticket is not included.
- **Christmas tree lighting:** Saturday, November 28, 5 p.m., Summit Backyard Plaza. Seasonal food and drink specials, hot chocolate, a fire and holiday sweets. Free with a lift ticket or membership.
- **Indoor storytime:** Mondays, November 30, December 7 and December 14, 10 to 10:30 a.m., Summit Lodge. Free hot chocolate and treats after. Free with a lift ticket or membership.
- **Gift shop offers:** Saturdays, November 28, December 5 and December 12, 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Members get 40 per cent off all items, including clothing, local art, home items, jewellery, stationery, soaps and candles.
- **Summit Surprises:** December 1 to 24. Follow photo clues on the gondola's social media, find the hidden spot at the summit and claim a prize. Prizes change daily and range from sweet treats and small gifts to experiences.

- Sea to Sky Gondola, 36800 Highway 99, Squamish

- Most activities are free with a lift ticket or membership
- Santa photos need to be booked in advance
- Phone: 778-266-1056

stories.head: Rainfall warning for Howe Sound Friday, and more storms are lined up
stories.dek: Heavy rain is on the way, and Environment Canada says it is the first storm in a series of wet and windy weather. A rainfall warning covers Howe Sound and parts of Metro Vancouver. Rain starts after midnight tonight and lasts through Friday, with up to 80 mm possible in some areas.
stories.take: Heavy rain starts after midnight tonight and lasts through Friday, so clear fallen leaves from nearby storm drains and watch for pooling water and washouts near rivers, creeks and culverts.
stories.body:
## What is coming

Environment Canada has issued a rainfall warning for Howe Sound. A strong low pressure system will bring heavy rain starting after midnight tonight. The rain is expected to continue through the day on Friday and taper off Friday evening.

Environment Canada says this is the first storm in a series of wet and windy weather ahead.

## How much rain

- Up to 80 mm for communities at higher elevations on the North Shore and communities near southern Howe Sound
- Closer to 50 mm for lower elevations and communities in northeast Metro Vancouver, including Coquitlam

The warning covers the North Shore (including West Vancouver and North Vancouver), northeast Metro Vancouver (including Coquitlam) and Howe Sound.

## What to watch for

- Water will likely pool on roads and in low lying areas
- Visibility may suddenly drop at times
- Some property damage is possible
- Watch for washouts near rivers, creeks and culverts

Environment Canada asks people to clear fallen leaves from storm drains in their neighbourhood to help reduce damage to property.

## Staying informed

Environment Canada asks residents to keep checking its alerts and forecasts. You can report severe weather by email to BCstorm@ec.gc.ca or by posting on social media with the tag #BCStorm.

See the current warning on the [Environment Canada warnings page](https://weather.gc.ca/warnings/index_e.html?prov=bc). For local weather, Highway 99 and river conditions, check our [today page](/today/). Background on how Squamish manages flood risk is on our [flood protection issue page](/issues/flood-protection/).

stories.head: Squamish Nation councillor steps down for his health. What happens next
stories.dek: Sinámḵin Jody Broomfield has resigned his seat on the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw (Squamish Nation) Council for personal and medical reasons. He told Council on November 4, with ceremony, and the resignation took effect right away. The Nation's Electoral Commission will guide the next steps for the empty seat.
stories.take: The Squamish Nation Council now has a vacant seat, and the Nation's Electoral Commission will guide what happens next, with more information to come.
stories.body:
## What happened

On November 4, Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw (Squamish Nation) Councillor Sinámḵin Jody Broomfield told the Nation's Council he is resigning his seat. He gave his resignation in a ceremony that morning. It took effect right away.

He said he is leaving for personal and medical reasons. The Nation said this is the right decision for him and his health, and that Council fully supports him.

## What happens to the seat

The Nation says that, under its laws and governance structure, its Electoral Commission has been called in to guide the next steps for the now vacant council seat. The Nation says it will share more information with its community shortly.

## In his own words

In a statement, Broomfield said serving the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh People "has been one of the greatest privileges of my life" and thanked people for their trust and support.

He said it was "a decision I have struggled with for some time and did not make lightly," and that he needs time to focus on his health.

He said he will keep being active in the community and will continue to serve his people in the best way he can, even though he is stepping away from the Council table.

To his fellow councillors, he wrote: "Continue pulling that canoe for our People in the right direction." He closed with "One heart, one mind" and "Chen kwenmatuniyap," which he translated as "I thank you all."

## Read more

- [Read the Squamish Nation's full statement](https://www.squamish.net/regarding-councillor-sinam%e1%b8%b5in-jody-broomfield/)

stories.head: New mayor promises to be judged on results. Here's what he says he'll fix
stories.dek: Mayor Sean Easton and six councillors took their oaths Tuesday night in a packed room. In his first speech, Easton named four things he says Squamish needs fixed and told residents to measure council on results, not plans. A former mayor also told the new council that staff work for them.
stories.take: Councillor Eric Andersen is acting mayor for November. Easton, Sarah Ellis and Andersen will represent Squamish on the regional district board. The first real votes come on November 17, with a 2027 budget drafted at a 10.4% tax increase still ahead.

stories.body:
## The four things he says he'll fix

In his first speech, Easton named four needs he heard from residents during the campaign. He asked to be judged on one question: "Did we meaningfully and measurably improve the quality of life for residents?" [Watch him say it](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PRDD-SFmhn0&t=1946s).

- **Housing that locals can afford.** His campaign promises: make developers hand over a bigger share of affordable homes, speed up the Pioneer Way supportive housing project, and pause approval of new developments unless they clearly make life better and more affordable. [Housing in Squamish](/issues/housing/)
- **More recreation, culture and arts.** His promise: negotiate with Woodfibre LNG for a new recreation centre with a pool and ice rink. On the same night, a Grade 12 student asked council to make the Brennan Park pool and rink a priority. [Brennan Park and recreation](/issues/brennan-park-and-recreation/)
- **Social and health services for all ages.** He did not name a specific plan for this on the night, and we track no campaign promise from him on it yet.
- **Transportation that works for different needs.** His promises: an express highway bus every 15 minutes, worked out with BC Transit and the Province, and a pause on new bike lane and sidewalk upgrades until residents are properly consulted. [Transit and Highway 99](/issues/transit-and-highway-99/)

He also promised to hold property taxes flat in 2027. District staff have drafted a 10.4% increase, and this council decides it. We check every one of these promises against how he actually votes on [his scorecard](/council/sean-easton/).

## Sworn in

Squamish's new council took office on Tuesday night, November 3, in a packed room at the Squamish Valley Golf Club. Bagpiper Devin Biln and members of the RCMP led the council in, and Allan Harry gave a Squamish Nation blessing.

Provincial Court Judge T. Hinkson, who sits in North Vancouver, swore in [Mayor Sean Easton](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PRDD-SFmhn0&t=735s) first, then each councillor: [Eric Andersen](/council/eric-andersen/), [Janice DesJardins](/council/janice-desjardins/), [Sarah Ellis](/council/sarah-ellis/), [Luc Perreault](/council/luc-perreault/), [Laura Prosko](/council/laura-prosko/) and [Shaun Veltkamp](/council/shaun-veltkamp/). Each promised to follow the conflict of interest rules, be accountable for their decisions, and be respectful of others. Andersen swore his oath on two Bibles his parents were given at their Canadian citizenship ceremony on November 20, 1964.

"Ladies and gentlemen, your new council," the judge said. The term runs four years, to the fall of 2030.

## More from Easton's first speech

Easton said he wants "purposeful government" that puts residents at the centre. [Watch his address](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PRDD-SFmhn0&t=1835s).

Listening and empathy are not enough, he said. Council should be measured on whether it "meaningfully and measurably" improved life for residents, and must not confuse "plans completed for a job well done." He promised to involve the people affected by each decision and to be open about how he decides.

"No one else is coming to save us," he said, ending on a line from psychiatrist Charles Johnston: doing what we have always done, only harder, will not solve today's problems.

## What each councillor said

- **[Eric Andersen](/council/eric-andersen/)**, the only returning member: council must keep its "house in order," look after taxpayers' money, and take responsibility itself rather than "passing the buck" to staff.
- **[Janice DesJardins](/council/janice-desjardins/)**: thanked her family, including her grandfather Alex Munro, and promised that Squamish Nation members who live in Squamish will be heard at the council table.
- **[Sarah Ellis](/council/sarah-ellis/)**: said many residents told her they are struggling with affordability and the pace of change, and some fear they won't be able to stay. She confirmed she is leaving her job as executive director of Housing Squamish.
- **[Luc Perreault](/council/luc-perreault/)**: spoke without notes. He said the council members bring very different backgrounds, and that different viewpoints are how council will succeed.
- **[Laura Prosko](/council/laura-prosko/)**: named growth, affordability, infrastructure and recreation, "like Brennan Park," as the big decisions ahead. She quoted her mother: you measure a person by what they actually do, not what they say they'll do.
- **[Shaun Veltkamp](/council/shaun-veltkamp/)**: thanked his family, who ran his campaign, and said he wants a stronger relationship with the Squamish Nation.

## Who got which job

Every appointment passed in one vote each, with no one voting against.

**Acting mayor** (stands in when the mayor is away):
- November 2026: Andersen
- December 2026: Ellis
- January 2027: Andersen
- February 2027: Ellis
- March 2027: Prosko
- April 2027: Perreault
- May 2027: Veltkamp
- June 2027: DesJardins
- July to December 2027: Andersen, Ellis, Prosko, Perreault, Veltkamp, DesJardins

**Squamish-Lillooet Regional District board:** Mayor Easton (5 votes), Ellis (4 votes) and Andersen (4 votes). Backups: Prosko, Perreault and Veltkamp.

**Squamish Library Board:** DesJardins.

**Community Forest Board:** Ellis and Perreault.

**Land Back Task Force:** Andersen, Prosko and Veltkamp. This is the group working with the Squamish Nation on returning land.

**2027 meetings:** council approved its [2027 meeting schedule](https://squamish.civicweb.net/document/271675/). Regular meetings are at 6 p.m. in Council Chambers at Municipal Hall.

## What residents asked council for

Each member invited one guest to speak.
- **Beau Smart**, a Grade 12 student at Howe Sound Secondary, asked council to support the arts and fix up the Eagle Eye Theatre, which he is raising money for. He also plugged *Oink*, a Between the Shifts Theatre play about Squamish, running November 26 to December 5.
- **Former mayor Corinne Lonsdale** told council that staff work for council, not the other way around, and urged members to "take back" authority handed to staff. She asked for a public meeting before second reading of any rezoning, surveys before big spending, and a newsletter in every mailbox every three months for people who aren't online.
- **Kirby Brown**, chair of Housing Squamish, praised Ellis and said Housing Squamish could only buy its first property through its partnership with the Squamish Nation's housing society.
- **Chief Dale Harry**, one of the Squamish Nation's 16 hereditary chiefs, asked council to build friendship and partnership with the Nation, and to "agree in how you disagree."
- **Lydia Prosko**, a Grade 12 student, said she could never finish swimming lessons because she couldn't get into programs. She asked council to make the Brennan Park pool and rink a priority and to bring more for youth to do.
- A friend of Veltkamp's family asked council for "the tough decisions, not the popular ones," and to avoid change for the sake of change.
- **Brett Easton**, the mayor's brother, said people on the campaign trail believe Squamish can be better.

stories.head: A BC Ferry killed Notcho the humpback. The Squamish Nation is laying him to rest
stories.dek: Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw (Squamish Nation) says Notcho, a male humpback whale, was hit and killed by a BC Ferry on October 18. His remains were found near Gambier Island on October 26 and brought to Squamish Nation territory. A team is harvesting what is usable, and a burial ceremony will be held at a later date.
stories.take: The Squamish Nation says a burial ceremony for Notcho will be held at a later date and asks people to check its website for updates.
stories.body:
## What happened

In a November 3 update, Squamish Nation Chairperson Sxwíxwtn Wilson Williams shared news about Notcho, a male humpback whale. The Nation understands he was hit and killed by a BC Ferry on October 18. His remains were found near Gambier Island on October 26.

In recent months, the Nation's Ta na wa Yúus ta Stitúyntsam̓ (Rights and Title) Department has been building ties with the Canadian Coast Guard and Fisheries and Oceans Canada. That work included sharing knowledge about the importance of whales in Squamish history and culture. Because of those ties, Notcho was brought to Squamish Nation territory so his remains could be cared for under the Nation's laws.

The Nation says receiving a whale in its territory is something its people have not known for many generations.

## Who helped

Several teams were put together quickly. The Nation thanked:

- Its Knowledge Keepers and Elders, and a Nuu-Chah-Nulth First Nation Elder who travelled to guide the process
- Squamish Nation staff from Rights and Title, Language and Culture, Intergovernmental Relations and Strategic Partnerships, Public Safety, and Nch'ḵay̓ Development Corporation
- Community members who came out to help
- Fisheries and Oceans Canada, the Canadian Coast Guard, CN and CN Police
- The City of Vancouver, including Councillor Sean Orr and Park Board Commissioner Tʼuyʼtʼtanat-Cease Wyss
- Metro Vancouver, Seaspan and Paladin Security

## What happens to the remains

A team has been working around the clock to harvest what is usable for the Nation's people. Everything harvested will be catalogued, stored and shared through the community according to the Nation's laws and teachings. The Nation plans to use Notcho's skeleton for educational and cultural purposes.

## What comes next

The work is ongoing. The Nation says it will share more in the coming weeks and months. A ceremony to mark Notcho's final burial on Squamish Nation territory will be held at a later date. No date has been announced.

Read the full update on the [Squamish Nation website](https://www.squamish.net/update-on-notcho-thank-you-for-honouring-our-practices/).

stories.head: Regional district waives fees for First Nations housing and cultural projects
stories.dek: The Squamish-Lillooet Regional District Board has adopted changes to its bylaw on development application fees and procedures. The changes let the regional district waive up to 100 per cent of fees for eligible First Nations affordable housing and traditional cultural activity projects. The bylaw was adopted at the board's October meeting after a referral to First Nations.
stories.take: Eligible First Nations affordable housing and traditional cultural activity projects on fee simple lands can now get up to 100 per cent off regional district development application fees.
stories.body:
## What changed

The Squamish-Lillooet Regional District Board adopted Amendment Bylaw No. 1969-2026 at its October board meeting. It updates the regional district's Development Approval Information, Fees and Notification Procedures Bylaw No. 1936-2025. The regional district says the changes apply to all of its areas.

The work came from the regional district's Indigenous Relations, Truth and Reconciliation Guide. The guide commits the regional district to review its policies, bylaws and procedures so they better reflect Indigenous perspectives and strengthen relationships with First Nations in the region.

## The key changes

- New definitions of "First Nations" and "Traditional Cultural Activity", written in response to First Nations feedback
- Clearer rules on archaeological information reports and following the Heritage Conservation Act
- New power to waive up to 100 per cent of development application fees for eligible First Nations affordable housing and traditional cultural activity projects on fee simple lands
- Clearer timelines for when development approvals and permits expire
- New cost recovery agreements for complex applications that need specialized technical review
- Other updates to make the bylaw easier to read and apply consistently

The regional district says asking for archaeological assessments earlier should help find possible issues sooner and give applicants more certainty.

## How First Nations were involved

The board gave the changes first and second reading in June 2026. The draft was then sent to all First Nations whose core traditional territories fall within the regional district. The regional district says the feedback it received shaped the final version.

Presiding Chair Jenna Stoner said the review let the regional district improve service for applicants while also putting its reconciliation commitments into practice. She said the feedback made the bylaw more effective and more transparent.

## More information

Read the full notice from the [Squamish-Lillooet Regional District](https://www.slrd.bc.ca/inside-slrd/news-notices/slrd-board-adopts-bylaw-amendments-improve-development-application). stories.head: Squamish starts work on its first urban forest strategy
stories.dek: The District of Squamish is developing its first Urban Forest Management Strategy. It will guide tree protection, planting and care on public and private land over the next 25 years. A community survey, an online mapping tool and an open house are planned, with details coming soon.
stories.take: Residents will be able to share their views through a survey, nominate valued or heritage trees on a map, and attend an open house once the District posts the details.
stories.body:
## What is happening

The District of Squamish is writing its first Urban Forest Management Strategy. The plan will guide how trees are protected, planted and cared for over the next 25 years. It covers both public and private land.

The urban forest includes trees in yards, along streets, in parks and school grounds, beside rivers and in natural areas. It also includes the soil and other plants that support those trees.

## Why the District says it is needed

As Squamish grows, protecting existing trees and making room for new ones takes coordination. That work spans streets, parks, natural areas and private properties. The District says tree management also has to deal with:

- climate change and wildfire risk
- wildlife habitat
- protecting waterways
- slope stability
- community needs

The strategy will help the District set priorities and plan the resources needed for long term tree care. It will also look at where more trees could give more people shade and access to nature.

## How to take part

The District lists three ways to get involved. Details for each are still to come.

- **Community survey** (coming soon): share what matters to you about local trees, the problems you see, and where efforts should focus.
- **Mapping tool** (coming soon): mark places and trees you value, suggest spots for planting or improvements, and nominate heritage or significant trees. Heritage trees are recognized under the District's Heritage Management Strategy.
- **Community open house** (more information soon): learn about the strategy, ask questions and share ideas.

Updates will be posted on the [Let's Talk Squamish urban forest page](https://letstalksquamish.ca/urban-forest).

## What comes next

Community input will be weighed together with feedback from the Squamish Nation, District Council and staff, and interested groups. The input will shape the strategy's vision, goals and actions. ## The local result

All 90 ballot boxes in West Vancouver to Sea to Sky have been counted in the initial count. Jeremy Valeriote of the BC Green Party is ahead. These are the preliminary numbers:

- BC Green Party (Jeremy Valeriote): 10,503 votes
- Conservative Party: 8,478 votes
- BC NDP (New Democratic Party): 2,283 votes
- All other candidates: 818 votes

That puts Valeriote 2,025 votes ahead of the Conservative candidate. Valeriote is one of only two Green candidates leading anywhere in B.C.

## Across British Columbia

Elections BC reports that 100 per cent of ballot boxes across the province have reported. The parties are leading in this many ridings:

- Conservative Party: 63 ridings, 862,688 votes (48.06 per cent)
- BC NDP: 28 ridings, 670,811 votes (37.37 per cent)
- BC Green Party: 2 ridings, 196,896 votes (10.97 per cent)

No other party is leading in any riding. CentreBC has 29,104 votes (1.62 per cent) and OneBC has 27,056 votes (1.51 per cent). Independent candidates have 3,202 votes in total.

In all, 1,799,550 votes were considered. There were 3,738,182 registered voters as of October 14, 2026. That makes the preliminary voter turnout 48.14 per cent.

## Why these results are not final

Elections BC says results from the initial count are preliminary. They can still change as they are checked for accuracy and completeness.

Some ballots have not been counted yet:

- Ballots sent by mail
- Absentee ballots

These will be counted at the final count. Elections BC does extra checks on these ballots to make sure only eligible voters vote, and that each person votes only once.

## What comes next

- Final count: November 6 to 10, 2026
- Results become official only when Elections BC declares them

If the final count matches the initial count, the riding's member of the Legislature will be a Green member sitting in opposition to a Conservative government.

You can follow the results on the [Elections BC results page](https://results.elections.bc.ca/).
